content: Consanguinity, derived from the Latin con(with) and sanguine (blood), refers to the condition of being from the same genetic lineage as another individual. It specifically denotes the quality of being descended from a common ancestor. This concept holds significant legal importance, as many jurisdictions consider consanguinity when determining whether two individuals are permitted to marry or when deciding inheritance rights in cases where a deceased person has not left a will. In legal terms, consanguinity is often represented in a genealogical chart, where each generation is depicted as a row. Individuals with a collateral consanguineous relationship share the same row. Relationships up to a certain degree of genetic relatedness (e.g., first cousins) are categorized as consanguineous. This threshold is chosen because the genetic impact of marriages between more distantly related individuals is generally minimal and comparable to that observed in the general population. Globally, the most common form of consanguineous union occurs between first cousins. In such unions, the spouses share one-eighth of their genes inherited from a common ancestor. Consequently, their offspring are homozygous (or more accurately, autozygous) at one-sixteenth of all genetic loci, which corresponds to an additional 6.25% homozygosity above the baseline level found in the general population. Legal Definitions In family law, consanguinity is crucial in defining who may legally marry. Some jurisdictions prohibit marriage between cousins, while others are more lenient, forbidding only unions between close relatives such as siblings, parents, or uncles and aunts. Additionally, many legal systems prevent individuals from serving on a jury if they share a certain degree of consanguinity with the defendant. In the context of intestate succession (when a person dies without a will), the Uniform Probate Code (Section 2-103) outlines the distribution of the estate. After the surviving spouse receives their share, the remainder is distributed to the descendants, which may include children, grandchildren, or great-grandchildren, whether biological or adopted. If there are no descendants, the estate passes to the decedent's parents. If neither descendants nor parents are present, the estate is distributed to the descendants of the decedent's parents, such as siblings, nieces, nephews, and their descendants. In the absence of these relatives, the property is passed to descendants of the decedent's grandparents, including uncles, aunts, first cousins, and more distant relatives. Most cultures define a degree of consanguinity below which sexual relationships are considered incestuous, often referred to as the prohibited degree of kinship. For example, in the Roman Catholic Church, unknowingly marrying a closely related blood relative is grounds for annulment. However, dispensations were frequently granted, especially during the period when the Church prohibited marriages within the fourth degree of relationship (first cousins) from 1550 to 1917. Before this, the prohibition extended to as much as the seventh degree of kinship. Adoption may or may not be legally recognized as creating a consanguineous bond. In most Western societies, adoptive relationships are treated as equivalent to blood relationships for these purposes. However, in other cultures, such as ancient Rome and Japan, it was common for a couple with only daughters to adopt a son-in-law, effectively creating a marriage between adoptive siblings. Among the Christian Habesha highlanders of Ethiopia and Eritrea (predominantly Orthodox Christian Amhara and Tigray-Tigrinya), it is a tradition to trace one's paternal ancestors back at least seven generations. This is because individuals with a common patrilineal ancestor within seven generations are considered brother and sister and are prohibited from marrying. The rule is less strict on the maternal side, where the limit is about four generations, but it is still determined patrilineally. This rule does not apply to Muslims or other ethnic groups in the region. Rates of Occurrence Historically, European nobles sometimes cited close degrees of consanguinity as a convenient reason for divorce, particularly in contexts where religious doctrine forbade the voluntary dissolution of an unhappy or childless marriage. Conversely, consanguinity laws of succession often require the next monarch to be of the same bloodline as the previous one, allowing, for example, illegitimate children to inherit the throne. According to the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, it is estimated that 55% of marriages among Muslims in the United Kingdom (and much of the Muslim world) are between first cousins. In these cases, preferential patrilateral parallel cousin marriage (where a boy marries his father's brother's daughter) is often favored.
